clue.text: Granary bread is short of a filling in my book? More than one!

parts.note: 'Cor!' is an exclamation of surprise, like 'My!'

indicators.note: the trimmed loaf fills the inside of the testament abbreviation

parts.note: NT, the New Testament, is a book made up of many books

indicators.note: being short of something means lacking it, so the letter named is dropped

parts.note: a loaf is a portion of bread

explanation.surface: A grumble that a slice of granary bread lacks a filling, then the joke that the speaker reckons there is more than one missing.
explanation.walkthrough: LOAF 'is short of a' becomes LOF, which goes 'filling in' NT; COR comes first. The exclamation 'More than one!' plays on the New Testament being a collection of books.
explanation.definitionFit: A corn loft is a storage room for grain, which is exactly what a granary is.

clue.text: Unemployment papers presented to not so welcoming nurse

parts.note: ID means identity papers

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in a guest, so the nurse goes inside

parts.note: less means not so much
EN is an Enrolled Nurse

explanation.surface: Someone out of work shows their papers to a nurse who is less than friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness is the state of having no work, a synonym for being without employment.

clue.text: National home with foundering listed? Maybe, I'm not sure

indicators.note: foundering means sinking and breaking up, so the letters are wrecked into a new order

parts.note: 'um' is the noise of someone hesitating, unsure

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a national home, listed as heritage, is sinking, and admits they don't know.
explanation.walkthrough: Wembley Stadium in London is the home ground of the England national football team.
explanation.definitionFit: The stadium is where the England national side plays its home matches, so it is the nation's sporting home.

clue.text: Reproduce the usual rubbish

parts.note: par means the normal or usual level
rot means nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: A complaint that reproductions always churn out the same old rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot is to repeat words mechanically, copying them as a parrot does.

clue.text: Will she do Bob doubles — or double?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a bell-..., who performs methods such as Plain Bob Doubles

explanation.walkthrough: Bob Doubles is a method in English church bell change-ringing; it sounds like a hairdo or a tennis match.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell-ringer pulls a church bell rope, and a dead ringer is a close lookalike of someone else.

clue.text: "Dad's botched Tower theft" as told by Colonel's son?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a father is a family member by birth

definitions.text: botched Tower theft" as told by Colonel's son
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an account (relation) of Colonel Blood's failed theft of the Crown Jewels, as his son would tell it

explanation.walkthrough: In 1671 Colonel Thomas Blood tried and failed to steal the Crown Jewels from the Tower of London; a relation is also an account or telling of events.
explanation.definitionFit: A father is kin by birth, which is what the phrase means; the second reading makes it Blood's story.

clue.text: Second scorer a reciprocal service provider

parts.note: to second a motion is to back it
one who scores a surface, marking it with lines, scratches it

explanation.surface: The second goalscorer in a match turns out to be someone who returns favours.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who scratches your back expecting you to scratch theirs trades favours, an idiom for mutual help.

clue.text: Privates hereabouts suffering for eternity?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a euphemism for the genitals
second meaning: hell, the underworld where souls suffer forever

explanation.walkthrough: 'Privates' suggests soldiers, but it is the coy word for the genitals.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a jokey euphemism for the genitals and also a literal name for the underworld of the damned.

clue.text: Screen a series of Stones concerts

indicators.note: series of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Something screened as part of a run of Rolling Stones gigs.
explanation.definitionFit: A sconce is a small fortification or protective screen, an old military sense of the word.

clue.text: Equitably acquire services of broadcaster?

indicators.note: a broadcaster speaks to listeners, so the words are taken as heard

parts.note: to acquire something is to buy it; religious services are rites

explanation.surface: A fair way to purchase the services of a TV or radio station.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something by rights means doing it properly and fairly, as justice would dictate.

clue.text: Love of a different sport, perhaps Holland crushing India

indicators.note: crushing pictures the outer letters squeezing the other inside them

parts.note: NL is the international code for the Netherlands, of which Holland is a part
I is India in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Holland beat India in some sport other than tennis, leaving the opposition with no score.
explanation.definitionFit: Love is a zero score in tennis; in football the same zero is called nil.

clue.text: To land on old nag, front of saddle repositioned

indicators.note: repositioned says that letter is lifted out and put back somewhere else in the word

parts.note: a-horse is an archaic word meaning on horseback

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter, here of saddle

explanation.surface: A rider on an old horse shifts the saddle forward before reaching land.
explanation.walkthrough: In A-HORSE the S is moved forward to follow the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Going ashore means going onto dry ground, i.e. to land from the sea.

clue.text: What's keen yet wavering operator finally pressed?

definitions.text: What's keen yet wavering operator finally pressed?

indicators.note: wavering means unsteady, so the letters shift into a new order
finally picks the last letter of operator

explanation.surface: An eager but hesitant computer operator finally presses a key to confirm.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: an operator, keen but hesitant, at last presses this key.
explanation.definitionFit: The key on a keyboard pressed to submit or confirm input is called by this name.

clue.text: Decline the love of Robert Browning originally?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to fall away or diminish

definitions.text: the love of Robert Browning originally
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the initials Elizabeth Barrett Browning, the poet's wife, signed with

explanation.surface: A question about whether Robert Browning's first love faded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' points to the initials of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, whom Robert Browning loved and married.
explanation.definitionFit: To ebb is to fall away or diminish, like the tide going out.

clue.text: 9, inside, it should have one "Quiet" sign installed

definitions.text: 9, inside, it should have one "Quiet" sign installed

indicators.note: inside says the following pieces go within the letters from 9
installed means fitted in, so the pieces are placed within

parts.note: the answer to 9-across, BY RIGHTS, reduced to BY and R R, two abbreviations for right
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral one
'sh!' is a call for quiet
Libra is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A national library that by rights ought to display a 'Quiet' sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 9's two words are opened up: B..Y holds R..R, the two rights, and the other pieces sit between the Rs. Fittingly, the library is a legal deposit library, entitled by right to a copy of every UK book.
explanation.definitionFit: The national library of the UK is a legal deposit library, entitled by law to a copy of each book.

clue.text: Cube root of 27? Ditto!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: three, written in Roman numerals
second meaning: the same as the answer to 27-across, an example of roman numerals

explanation.walkthrough: '27' looks like just a number, but 'Ditto' says to read it again as the clue reference: III is itself Roman numerals, the answer to 27-across.
explanation.definitionFit: Three cubed is twenty-seven, and the Roman way of writing three is an instance of Roman numerals.

clue.text: See 14
Setter speaks ill of 25 resident?

definitions.note: a resident of Shetland, the answer to 25-across

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as I
to slander is to speak falsely and damagingly of someone

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to badmouthing someone from Shetland.
explanation.definitionFit: Shetland is a group of islands, so anyone living there is an island dweller.

clue.text: Way to get round unopened Soave shared at cruciverbal gathering?

indicators.note: what crossword solvers share at a meetup is their shorthand, so the letters are read as clue-writers' codes

parts.note: Soave, an Italian white wine, without its opening letter is OAVE, which crossword solvers sharing their shorthand read as O (a ring) and AVE (avenue, a road)

explanation.surface: Getting round a bottle of Soave, still unopened, to share at a crossword meetup.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer's pieces, ring and road, would be clued in crosswords as O and AVE, which together spell Soave minus its S. Soave is an Italian white wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring road circles a town so traffic can go round the centre rather than through it.

clue.text: See 3
Frank pictures from the East in spectator's range

indicators.note: in says the reversed pictures sit inside the range of view

parts.note: sight is the distance a viewer can see

indicators.note: read from the east, i.e. right to left in an across clue, the word runs backwards

parts.note: pictures are works of art

explanation.surface: Frank's paintings from the Orient are within a viewer's field of vision.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frank means speaking honestly and directly, which is what being straight with someone is.

clue.text: A sharp change, end of summer to middle of November, approximately

definitions.text: A sharp change, end of summer to middle of November, approximately

indicators.note: 'to' says the last letter of summer is changed to the letter from November

parts.note: a U-turn is an abrupt reversal of direction or policy

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, here of summer
the middle of a word is its central letter, here of November
November has eight letters and no single middle, so the letter taken is only roughly central

explanation.surface: A sudden swing in the weather, from late summer into mid-November roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: A U-TURN has its R (end of summer) changed to M (middle of November, roughly, as the word has no single middle letter). The whole clue also describes the season.
explanation.definitionFit: The season after summer runs roughly from late September to November in the northern hemisphere.

clue.text: Are blurred pictures like this in Warhol's dismal frames?

indicators.note: frames means surrounds, so the dull colour goes round the word in

parts.note: Andy Warhol was American, and the American spelling of grey, meaning dismal, is gray

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Warhol's gloomy framed pictures are blurry.
explanation.definitionFit: Grainy images show a coarse speckled texture and lack sharpness, typical of poor or enlarged photos.

clue.text: 50-year-old journo's rate of pay?

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for 50
being so many years old means that number in age

explanation.surface: A veteran fifty-year-old journalist and their pay rate.
explanation.walkthrough: A fifty-year-old is L in age, with L read as the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Linage is payment to a writer at so much per line printed, as freelance journalists were once paid.

clue.text: Off limits, "nosy" guy

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its ends, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: nosy here means of the nose, i.e. nasal

explanation.surface: A man told to keep his nose out because it is off limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nosy' looks like prying, but here it means to do with the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Asa is a man's given name, and a guy is any man.

clue.text: Where beach borders the shimmering loch's edge?

definitions.text: Where beach borders the shimmering loch's edge?

indicators.note: borders means lies around the edges of, so the other letters go inside

parts.note: sand is what a beach is made of

indicators.note: shimmering means wavering in the light, so these letters are reshuffled
the edge here is the first letter of loch's

explanation.surface: Somewhere a sandy beach fringes a glittering Scottish loch.
explanation.walkthrough: Shetland is the island group north of mainland Scotland, full of lochs and beaches; a loch is a Scottish lake.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shetland Islands are a Scottish archipelago where shore and loch lie side by side.

clue.text: Strait hurried through on return river journey?

indicators.note: on return says the word is read coming back, from the end

parts.note: to run through something is to hurry through it
a row is a trip in a rowing boat on a river

explanation.surface: Rushing up a channel and back on a boat trip down the river.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow is a constricted stretch of water, usually in the plural, similar to a strait.

clue.text: Civil, I did mild mix, showing them all up

definitions.text: Civil, I did mild mix, showing them all up

parts.words: Civil, I did mild mix, showing them all up
parts.note: every letter of the four words before 'showing' is one of the Roman number symbols, so the words display them all

explanation.walkthrough: Civil, I, did, mild and mix are spelt only from C, I, V, L, D, M and X, which between them are all seven Roman number letters.
explanation.definitionFit: C, D, I, L, M, V and X are the complete set of symbols the ancient Romans used for numbers.
